title: Stars, galaxies and the universe
lede: How stars shine, live and die, why you're made of material forged inside them, and how we know the universe began 13.8 billion years ago.

sections.md:
## What a star is
A **star** is a giant ball of hot gas held together by its own gravity. In its **core**, pressure and temperature are so extreme (the Sun's core is about **15 million °C**) that hydrogen atoms smash together and fuse into **helium**. That's **nuclear fusion**.

Fusion converts a tiny bit of mass into a huge amount of energy, which is what Einstein's **E = mc²** describes: energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. Because c² is enormous, a little mass makes a lot of energy. The Sun turns about **4 million tons** of mass into energy **every second**, and it has enough fuel to keep going for billions of years.

A star's life is a balance: **gravity** squeezes inward; the **energy from fusion** pushes outward.

## Reading a star's color
A star's color tells you its **surface temperature**, the same way a stove burner glows red, then orange, then white as it heats up.

| Color | Surface temperature | Example |
|---|---|---|
| red | ~3,000 °C (coolest) | Betelgeuse, most small stars |
| orange | ~4,000 °C | Arcturus |
| yellow-white | ~5,500 °C | the Sun |
| white | ~10,000 °C | Sirius |
| blue | 20,000 °C+ (hottest) | Spica |

Surprising to most people: **blue stars are hotter than red ones**.

sections.q: Which star is hottest at its surface?
sections.why: Blue = hottest; red = coolest. The opposite of the hot/cold colors on a faucet.

sections.md:
## The life of a star: mass decides everything
Every star is born in a **nebula**, a cloud of gas and dust, when gravity pulls a clump together until its core ignites fusion.

**Sun-like stars:**
**nebula → main-sequence star** (fusing hydrogen for billions of years) **→ red giant** (swells up as the core runs low) **→ planetary nebula** (outer layers drift away) **→ white dwarf** (a hot, Earth-sized leftover core that slowly cools)

**Massive stars** (more than about 8 times the Sun):
**nebula → main sequence** (shorter: they burn fuel much faster) **→ red supergiant → supernova** (a colossal explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy) **→ neutron star** or, for the biggest, **black hole**

The Sun is about **4.6 billion years** old, roughly halfway through its life. In about 5 billion years it will become a red giant.

## You are made of star stuff
The Big Bang produced mostly **hydrogen and helium**. Nearly all the heavier elements, the **carbon** in your cells, the **oxygen** you breathe, the **calcium** in your bones and the **iron** in your blood, were made later, by fusion inside stars and in their explosive deaths, then scattered into space to form new stars and planets.

Astronomer Carl Sagan put it simply: *we are made of star-stuff.* That's not poetry. It's chemistry.

## Measuring cosmic distance
A **light-year** is a **distance**, not a time: how far light travels in one year, about **9.5 trillion km** (5.9 trillion miles).

- The nearest star beyond the Sun, **Proxima Centauri**, is about **4.2 light-years** away. Its light left before you finished your last few birthdays.
- Looking far is looking **back in time**. You see stars as they were when their light left them.

## Galaxies
A **galaxy** is a vast system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity.

- Our galaxy, the **Milky Way**, is a **barred spiral** about **100,000 light-years** across, with **hundreds of billions** of stars. The Sun sits in a spiral arm about 26,000 light-years from the center, where a supermassive black hole sits.
- Galaxy shapes: **spiral** (pinwheel), **elliptical** (smooth, oval), **irregular** (no clear shape).
- Our nearest large neighbor, the **Andromeda Galaxy**, is about **2.5 million light-years** away. On a dark night it's one of the most distant things you can see with your naked eyes, and the light you see left it before our species existed.
- The observable universe holds **hundreds of billions** of galaxies, possibly more.

## The Big Bang
About **13.8 billion years ago**, the universe was extremely hot and dense, and it has been **expanding** and cooling ever since. Three key pieces of evidence:

1. **Galaxies are moving apart.** In 1929, **Edwin Hubble** showed that farther galaxies are moving away faster. Their light is stretched toward red (**redshift**), like the falling pitch of a passing siren. Run the movie backward and everything was once together.
2. **The cosmic microwave background.** In 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected a faint microwave glow coming from every direction: the cooled-down afterglow of the early hot universe.
3. **The mix of elements.** The amounts of hydrogen and helium in the universe match what the Big Bang theory predicts.

It wasn't an explosion **inside** space. It was the expansion **of space itself**, everywhere at once.

sections.title: How old is the light?
sections.problem: A galaxy is 50 million light-years away. When did the light you see today leave it?
steps: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year.
50 million light-years away → the light traveled 50 million years.
sections.answer: **50 million years ago**, after the dinosaurs died out (about 66 million years ago). If that galaxy vanished today, we wouldn't know for 50 million years.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **A light-year is a distance**, not a time.
- **Stars don't burn like fire.** Fire is chemical; stars are nuclear fusion. Space has no oxygen for fire.
- **Black holes aren't cosmic vacuum cleaners.** From far away, a black hole's gravity acts like any object of the same mass. If the Sun became one (it can't: too small), Earth's orbit wouldn't change.
- **The Big Bang didn't happen at one point in space.** Space itself expanded.

practice.q: Redshift of distant galaxies shows the universe is…
The iron in your blood was originally made…
practice.why: Heavy elements are forged by stars.

practice.q: Star A is red, star B is blue. Which is true?
practice.why: Blue = hotter surface, like a flame or a heated piece of metal moving from red to white to blue-white.
practice.hint: Think of metal heated in a forge.

practice.q: A massive star burns for about 10 million years; the Sun for about 10 billion. Why does the bigger star die so much sooner?
options: Its stronger gravity squeezes the core harder, so it burns its fuel much faster
practice.why: More mass means more fuel, but the extra gravity drives fusion **so much** faster that it runs out first. Big engines burn fuel fastest.
practice.hint: More gravity → more pressure → faster fusion.

practice.q: Proxima Centauri is 4.2 light-years away. A light-year is about 9.5 trillion km. About how many **trillion** km away is it? (1 decimal)
practice.why: 4.2 × 9.5 = **39.9 trillion km**. Even our fastest spacecraft would need thousands of years to get there.
practice.hint: Multiply light-years by km per light-year.

practice.q: If the Sun suddenly vanished, how long until Earth went dark?
practice.why: The last light already on its way would keep arriving for about 8 minutes 20 seconds. (Gravity's change also travels at light speed, so Earth's orbit wouldn't change until then either.)
practice.hint: How long does sunlight take to reach us?
